title: Why Good Students Fail: And Why Neither Grit nor Human Tutoring is Enough
author: Alfred Essa
summary: Essa retells Clark Glymour's account of failing every Black student in his first Princeton logic course in 1969. Glymour concluded the fault lay in his course design rather than his students: lectures assumed prior mastery, and one-shot high-stakes exams gave no chance to recover. He rebuilt the course around short chapters, many short penalty-free tests, immediate feedback and brief check-ins, and the same cohort went from failing to all As and Bs. Essa's move is to show that neither grit nor ordinary tutoring fixes a badly designed course, and that mastery-style design needs a scale that only computer-based instruction can supply. He ends by suggesting that AI combined with serious course redesign might finally address this long-standing problem.
points: Glymour's key diagnostic question is whether a course design gives underprepared students an opportunity to catch up.
Grit alone cannot substitute for missing background when lectures presume everything before them was understood and assessment is one-shot.
The redesign used small chapters, many parallel short tests, immediate feedback and no penalty for failed attempts, producing As and Bs for the same group that had failed.
Glymour found the approach physically unsustainable for one instructor, which Essa uses to argue for computer-assisted delivery alongside human teachers.
quotes: The course organization gave students little opportunity to substitute sweat for background; the lectures presumed they had followed everything up to the point of the lecture; if they hadn’t, they would be lost.
Does the course design give underprepared students an opportunity to catch up?
A test was immediately graded; if failed, the student would take another test on the same material after a two-day wait. No student took the very same test twice.
What was the result of the redesigned course? Although the same number of black students enrolled as the previous semester, this time half of them earned an A and the others all received a B grade.
The computer could be programmed with small modules, with interactive questions and prompts, with many penalty-free tests for each module, even with automated problem-solving aids.
